text: Numbers are the easy part. Real data has names with stray spaces, emails in mixed case, and phone numbers in five formats. And text that does not match cannot be joined: an email with a trailing space will never equal the clean one. The dot str accessor is how pandas cleans text at scale.

Four jobs cover most text work. Clean, with strip, lower, title and replace. Split, to break a string into pieces. Search, with contains. And extract, to pull out a pattern with a regular expression. Each runs on the whole column at once.

Here is an illustrative messy contact table. Strip removes stray whitespace, and lower fixes the case. Chain them, because each step returns a Series that supports dot str again. A regex replace of backslash s plus collapses double spaces. Always pass regex equals True or False explicitly, since the default has changed between pandas versions. Missing values pass through untouched.

Split breaks a string at a separator. Split an email at the at sign, take piece one with dot str bracket one, and you have the domain. Value counts on it shows three example dot com addresses. Contains gives a True or False mask for filtering. One trap: on a column with missing values it returns a missing result, so pass na equals False.

Extract pulls out whatever matches the groups in parentheses, one column per group. A few patterns cover most data work: backslash d is a digit, backslash capital D is a non-digit, backslash s is whitespace, plus means one or more. You do not need to master regular expressions today.

Here is a worked example. Phone numbers arrive with parentheses, dashes, dots and spaces. Replace every non-digit with nothing, then check the length. All five are ten digits, so every number is complete. A nine or eleven would be a red flag. That kind of deliberate check is the seed of Chapter 5.
Clean text makes joins and counts trustworthy. Next up: Chapter 5, data cleaning, beginning with missing data: diagnosis and handling.
